extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism; newsroom editors, producers, and journalists interested in news judgment and story selection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how journalists, editors, and producers decide which items become news across television and newsmagazines, including criteria of importance, interest, medium/format fit, novelty, and product constraints. Emphasizes practical newsroom trade-offs (space, pictures, action, audience) and story types editors favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance (national / large-scale impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are chosen when they meet importance considerations — e.g., federal law and the federal government, education affecting large numbers, or violations of national values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-of-the-book sections favor items of national importance; legal and education sections easily apply these considerations. Examples: federal government actions, Supreme Court decisions, education issues that affect many people. Anti-pattern: relying on parochial or trivial local concerns for front-page treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience enthusiasm / touch large numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: When ranking importance, editors often prefer stories that 'touch large numbers of people' to evoke audience interest and increase appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top producers will choose stories likely to interest large audiences (e.g., Jaws was chosen because audience enthusiasm was assured). Use when no single 'importance' clearly dominates. Anti-pattern: selecting stories of narrow interest that will not attract viewers/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional-source-determined importance vs audience-determined importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections such as science, medicine, and the arts may apply importance as defined by professional leaders (major sources) rather than immediate audience interest; conflict between these perspectives is endemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers defer to professional judgments for specialized sections but top editors also prefer impact on large numbers. Historical consideration: do not ignore 'far-out' ideas that may later become significant (e.g., Freud, Darwin). Balance professional esteem with potential audience impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizability for covers / confer national recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazine covers must feature individuals or subjects that are easily recognized as well as important; unfamiliar or 'dry' subjects are at a disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers serve to assign national importance and provide recognition; popular entertainers and well-known figures are favored. Example: Nabokov made Time's cover only after a top editor overruled concerns about public unfamiliarity. Anti-pattern: running covers on obscure figures that won't resonate with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selecting covers that imply endorsement or influence outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors avoid cover choices that could be taken as influencing political outcomes or as the magazine's endorsement of a candidate, especially for controversial figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Eugene McCarthy was postponed/rejected for cover placement because editors feared influencing the Democratic convention or being read as endorsing him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting stories as balance and replacements
rubrics_metrics.description: Interesting stories (often 'people stories') are used to balance 'bad' important news and provide timeless material usable as last-minute fill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interesting stories are chosen because editors assume selector enthusiasm implies audience interest; they are often decided by group taste. Use when filling gaps or to provide lighter/positive news. Anti-pattern: labeling a story 'interesting' despite group rejection — if anyone calls it 'boring' it likely will be dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: People stories (people acting or being acted upon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories featuring ordinary people in unusual situations or public officials behaving 'like people' rather than politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grant the audience a glimpse of private persona (e.g., presidential family activities). They are prototypical 'interesting' stories and often favored as closers or human-focused pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-reversal stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories where people depart from expected roles (man-bites-dog), e.g., a professor who becomes a janitor or criminals who reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be humorous or serious; valued for surprise and human interest. Use as a genre of interest-driven reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest stories
rubrics_metrics.description: People stories where ordinary people undergo experiences that evoke sympathy, pity, or admiration (victims of illness, heroes in disasters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selectors choose them because the audience can 'identify' with victims/heroes; these stories are emotionally moving to both selectors and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Short pieces that report and implicitly condemn actors or activities that violate enduring values (callous bureaucrats, corporate desecration, malfunctioning systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used as miniature editorials or critical items (e.g., Time's Americana, Newsweek's Nation items). Serve to highlight wrongdoing and feed moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of ordinary people overcoming villains or nature (adventurers, record-setters) that demonstrate resilience or human triumph without causing harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued as uplifting interest pieces and often used to close programs or sections on a positive note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gee‑whiz stories (surprise / novelty items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual category for stories that evoke surprise: unusual fads, cults, distinctive vocations, or oddities (e.g., hen laying green eggs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are typically not highly important but are entertaining and usable as fillers or closers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product considerations: 'Is it new? Is it good? Does it contribute to a well-balanced program?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists ask three core product questions while judging stories: novelty, quality, and contribution to overall program balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations are applied to every story and help choose among items of equal substantive merit; they also contain built-in audience-attracting devices so editors need not always explicitly 'think about' audience taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium considerations: television immediacy and film suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Television judges stories for whether they lend themselves to filming and to provide 'immediacy'; film is the medium's competitive weapon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers prioritize 'action' (incident or emotion) and avoid undramatic film and 'talking heads.' When film is unavailable, 'tell' stories are used, but producers prefer film when possible. Anti-pattern: prioritizing exciting film over substantive importance (sensationalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'action' for television film
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is 'something happening' — an incident, interpersonal conflict, people struggling, or strong emotion — and is the prime measure of film quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select film with clear action; dull film is less desirable, but for important stories, dull film is better than none. Anti-pattern: using undramatic film that fails to illustrate the story's point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium considerations: newsmagazine 'color' and 'prose pictures' / photographs as story drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmagazines seek 'color' and an array of details and dramatic quotes to create 'prose pictures'; still pictures are as important as text and can drive story choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors 'lead with a strong picture to catch the reader'; when stories are lesser in importance, strong photos may tip selection. Example: a debate where a top editor preferred artists who photographed better over those judged best by a writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format considerations: story structure (lead, narrative, closer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story must include a lead (a 'hook' stating an empirical highlight or moral issue), a narrative that documents/illustrates the lead (often via case study), and a closer that assesses significance or offers resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This format concretizes medium considerations and signals importance levels. Leads should attract attention; narratives supply illustration (film or body); closers provide some resolution or re-evaluation of expectations. Anti-pattern: stories lacking a point or ending may be dropped or shortened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format considerations: brevity and prescribed lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Formats impose prescribed lengths for tell stories, film, and features; brevity is a principal constraint because viewers/readers lose interest in long stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television and magazines favor short pieces; stories needing lengthy description/explanation are sometimes dropped (historically economic stories). Producers/writers avoid overly long items except when of unusual importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story must be transformable into a story with a point (avoid inconclusive pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: News becomes suitable only when transformed into a story with a point or ending; stories 'which do not make a point' or lack an ending can be dropped or relegated to brief telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced reporters can usually find a point or construct an ending for dramatic but inconclusive film; magazines have more freedom to develop endings than television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty: internal novelty and timeliness constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is central to news and judged by whether a story is new to journalists (internal novelty); time between deadlines circumscribes novelty, but exceptions exist for features and 'shelf' stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard news may use film shot a day or two earlier if accompanied by a recent tell story; features can stay longer. Journalists also create novelty by being ahistorical and treating events as discrete new happenings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space/section constraints and pre-killing
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited space (columns, segments) and fixed section mandates lead to exclusionary choices: back-of-the-book sections have few columns and are at risk of 'prekilling' when no sufficiently interesting/important stories exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: front-of-book allotted 21–24 columns; back-of-book often 3–6 columns. Editors may ignore scholarly books, poetry, and first novels for reviews. To avoid prekill, senior editors may be assigned back-of-book responsibilities or must find 'bright shorts' (75–100 words) to fill gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/packaging can determine story choice (photo-driven selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of strong pictures (especially with color) can lead editors to select stories that justify those images, sometimes overriding pure merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a strong picture 'to catch the reader'; with advent of color, top editors sometimes prefer photographers' subjects. Anti-pattern: choosing weaker substantive stories solely to justify a picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism: film must justify substantive importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Using exciting action film for stories that are substantively unimportant is condemned as sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should ensure the narrative justifies dramatic film; if only film is exciting but the underlying story lacks importance, pairing may be criticized as sensationalistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell stories and the importance of the textual 'lead' (text can be the real story)
rubrics_metrics.description: When film is unavailable or secondary, the reporter's narrative (text/tell story) often constitutes the actual story; television is 'visual radio' but words remain essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell stories supplement film and can stand independently; anchors draw audience and programs allot a portion of time specifically for tell stories (e.g., CBS 'magic number' of 6–8 minutes when Cronkite anchored). Ensure strong narration when film is weak or absent.
